did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job begins his first speech after seven days of silence by cursing the day of his birth, rather than directly cursing God.
Did you know? Job distinguishes between the day of his birth and the night when it was said, “A man has been conceived”—the night when a human being was formed.
Did you know? Job wishes for the day of his birth to be dark and for it not to be sought or remembered from above; in this way, he expresses a desire for that day to be erased from existence.
Did you know? Job mentions the “cursers of the day” and those who can rouse Leviathan, asking them to curse the day on which he was born.
Did you know? Job asks why he did not die in the womb or at birth, expressing the depth of his despair and his wish that he had never come into the world.
Did you know? Job describes death as a place of rest and quiet, where he would lie alongside kings, counselors, and wealthy princes.

Did you know? In his description of the place of death, Job presents it as a place where the wicked cease from troubling others, the weary find rest, and prisoners no longer hear the voice of their taskmaster.
Did you know? Job emphasizes that in the place of death there is no distinction between the small and the great, and the slave is free from his master.
Did you know? Job asks why light and life are given to those who suffer, and describes the longing for death and the joy of finding a grave.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Job says that he has found no peace, quiet, or rest; instead, trouble has come upon him, and he testifies that the fear he dreaded has come true.
